claim: Human calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a G-protein-coupled receptor that maintains Ca2+ homeostasis in serum.
source: Human calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a G-protein-coupled receptor that maintains Ca2+ homeostasis in serum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of CaSR, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: CaSR maintains Ca2+ homeostasis by the modulation of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion from parathyroid cells and the regulation of Ca2+ reabsorption by the kidney.
source: It maintains Ca2+ homeostasis by the modulation of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion from parathyroid cells and the regulation of Ca2+ reabsorption by the kidney (Brown, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown, 2013.

claim: CaSR is also a phosphate sensor that can sense moderate changes in extracellular phosphate concentration.
source: Recently, it has been reported that CaSR is also a phosphate sensor that can sense moderate changes in extracellular phosphate concentration (Centeno et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Dysfunctions of CaSR or mutations in its genes may lead to Ca2+ homeostatic disorders, such as familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism, and autosomal dominant hypocalcemia.
source: Dysfunctions of CaSR or mutations in its genes may lead to Ca2+ homeostatic disorders, such as familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism, and autosomal dominant hypocalcemia (Hendy et al., 2009; Pollak et al., 1993; Ward et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: CaSR belongs to the family C GPCR that includes gamma-aminobutyric acid B (GABAB) receptors, metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs), taste receptors, GPRC6a, and several orphan receptors.
source: CaSR belongs to the family C GPCR that includes gamma-aminobutyric acid B (GABAB) receptors, metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs), taste receptors, GPRC6a, and several orphan receptors (Ellaithy et al., 2020; Hannan et al., 2018; Heaney and Kinney, 2016; Pin and Bettler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CaSR functions as a disulphide-linked homodimer.
source: Like most class C GPCRs, CaSR functions as a disulphide-linked homodimer.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of CaSR, consistent with established knowledge of class C GPCRs.

claim: Each subunit of CaSR is comprised of a large extracellular domain (ECD) that contains a ligand-binding Venus flytrap (VFT) domain and a cysteine rich domain (CRD), and a seven-transmembrane domain (7TMD) that connects to CRD to carry signals from VFT domain to downstream G proteins.
source: Each subunit of CaSR is comprised of a large extracellular domain (ECD) that contains a ligand-binding Venus flytrap (VFT) domain and a cysteine rich domain (CRD), and a seven-transmembrane domain (7TMD) that connects to CRD to carry signals from VFT domain to downstream G proteins (Geng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CaSR can be activated or modulated by Ca2+ ions, amino acids.
source: CaSR can be activated or modulated by Ca2+ ions, amino acids (Geng et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016), L-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronorharman-3-carboxylic acid (TNCA), a tryptophan derivative ligand (Zhang et al., 2016), and several commercial calcium mimetic drugs, such as cinacalcet (Leach et al., 2016; Nemeth et al., 2004), etelcalcetide, and evocalcet (positive allosteric modulator, PAM, of CaSR) that are used for patients with end-stage kidney diseases undergoing dialysis (Alexander et al., 2015; Leach et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: TNCA is a tryptophan derivative ligand that can activate or modulate CaSR.
source: CaSR can be activated or modulated by Ca2+ ions, amino acids (Geng et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016), L-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronorharman-3-carboxylic acid (TNCA), a tryptophan derivative ligand (Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Cinacalcet, etelcalcetide, and evocalcet are positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of CaSR used for patients with end-stage kidney diseases undergoing dialysis.
source: several commercial calcium mimetic drugs, such as cinacalcet (Leach et al., 2016; Nemeth et al., 2004), etelcalcetide, and evocalcet (positive allosteric modulator, PAM, of CaSR) that are used for patients with end-stage kidney diseases undergoing dialysis (Alexander et al., 2015; Leach et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The crystal structures of the resting and active conformations of CaSR ECD were solved by two different groups.
source: The crystal structures of the resting and active conformations of CaSR ECD were solved by two different groups (Geng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: Ling et al. have solved the cryo-EM structures of full-length CaSR in active and inactive states.
source: More recently, Ling et al. have solved the cryo-EM structures of full-length CaSR in active and inactive states; however, their inactive structures do not show the fully inactive state and exhibit some characteristics of the active conformation of crystal CaSR ECD (Ling et al., 2021; Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ling et al., 2021.

claim: The inactive structures reported by Ling et al. do not show the fully inactive state and exhibit some characteristics of the active conformation of crystal CaSR ECD.
source: More recently, Ling et al. have solved the cryo-EM structures of full-length CaSR in active and inactive states; however, their inactive structures do not show the fully inactive state and exhibit some characteristics of the active conformation of crystal CaSR ECD (Ling et al., 2021; Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ling et al. structures based on comparison with crystal structures.

claim: In the active structures reported by Ling et al., Ca2+ ions and L-Trp work cooperatively to activate CaSR, leading to the closure of VFT domain.
source: In their active structures, they proposed that Ca2+ ions and L-Trp work cooperatively to activate CaSR, leading to the closure of VFT domain.
evidence: This is a description of the proposal made by Ling et al. in their study.

claim: The authors obtained cryo-EM structures of full-length CaSR in inactive and agonist+PAM bound conformations.
source: In our study, we used cryo-EM to obtain the structures of full-length CaSR in inactive and agonist+PAM bound conformations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The fully inactive structure is stabilized by a negative allosteric nanobody.
source: The fully inactive structure is stabilized by a negative allosteric nanobody.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental approach described in the manuscript.

claim: A new calcium binding site was identified at the interdomain cleft of VFT in the agonist+PAM bound structure.
source: In the agonist+PAM bound structure, we identified a new calcium binding site at the interdomain cleft of VFT, with Ca2+ and TNCA constitute a composite agonist to stabilize the closure of the VFT, leading to the conformational changes of the 7TMDs to initiate signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural data.

claim: Ca2+ and TNCA constitute a composite agonist to stabilize the closure of the VFT.
source: In the agonist+PAM bound structure, we identified a new calcium binding site at the interdomain cleft of VFT, with Ca2+ and TNCA constitute a composite agonist to stabilize the closure of the VFT, leading to the conformational changes of the 7TMDs to initiate signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural and functional data.

claim: NB-2D11 significantly inhibited the activity of CaSR with IC50 of 41.7 nM.
source: Of the several CaSR binders, NB-2D11 and NB88 significantly inhibited the activity of CaSR with IC50 of 41.7 nM and 167.1 nM, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular Ca2+ flux assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NB88 significantly inhibited the activity of CaSR with IC50 of 167.1 nM.
source: Of the several CaSR binders, NB-2D11 and NB88 significantly inhibited the activity of CaSR with IC50 of 41.7 nM and 167.1 nM, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular Ca2+ flux assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NB-2D11 demonstrated high-affinity binding to CaSR with KD of 0.24 nM.
source: Using surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to measure binding kinetics, both nanobodies NB-2D11 and NB88 demonstrated high-affinity binding to CaSR with KD of 0.24 nM and 3.9 nM, respectively (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NB88 demonstrated high-affinity binding to CaSR with KD of 3.9 nM.
source: Using surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to measure binding kinetics, both nanobodies NB-2D11 and NB88 demonstrated high-affinity binding to CaSR with KD of 0.24 nM and 3.9 nM, respectively (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Two active conformations of CaSR were observed with overall resolutions of 2.99 Å and 3.43 Å.
source: We have observed two active conformations with overall resolutions of 2.99 Å and 3.43 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results.

claim: Local refinement of ECDs and TMDs separately resulted in maps with resolutions of 3.07 Å and 4.3 Å, respectively.
source: We performed local refinement of ECDs and TMDs separately to obtain maps with resolutions of 3.07 Å and 4.3 Å, respectively, with quality density throughout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Table 1.

claim: Three conformations of inactive CaSR were observed with overall resolutions of 5.79 Å, 6.88 Å, and 7.11 Å.
source: Cryo-EM data present three conformations of inactive CaSR with an overall resolution of 5.79 Å, 6.88 Å, and 7.11 Å, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Local refinement focusing on the ECDs and the 7TMDs of inactive CaSR was performed separately to improve the resolutions to 4.5 Å and 4.8 Å, respectively.
source: The local refinement focusing on the ECDs and the 7TMDs was performed separately to improve the resolutions to 4.5 Å and 4.8 Å, respectively, with quality density throughout (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A; Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data processing results.

claim: The overall structures in the inactive and agonist+PAM bound states are homodimeric arrangement, in which two subunits almost parallelly interact in a side-by-side manner while facing opposite directions.
source: The overall structures in the inactive and agonist+PAM bound states are homodimeric arrangement, in which two subunits almost parallelly interact in a side-by-side manner while facing opposite directions.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The agonist+PAM bound structure of CaSR displays a substantial compaction compared to the inactive structure, including the reduction of length, height, and width.
source: The agonist+PAM bound structure of CaSR displays a substantial compaction compared to the inactive structure, including the reduction of length, height, and width.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two structures obtained in this study.

claim: In the agonist+PAM bound structure, both VFT modules adopt closed–closed conformation.
source: both VFT modules adopt closed–closed conformation, and the TNCA and Ca2+ ion composite is bound at the interdomain cleft between LB1 domain and LB2 domain (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: The TNCA and Ca2+ ion composite is bound at the interdomain cleft between LB1 domain and LB2 domain in the agonist+PAM bound structure.
source: both VFT modules adopt closed–closed conformation, and the TNCA and Ca2+ ion composite is bound at the interdomain cleft between LB1 domain and LB2 domain (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: The overall conformation of the agonist+PAM bound structure is consistent with the recently reported active conformation of the Ca2+/L-Trp-bound structure of CaSR (CaSRAcc).
source: The overall conformation of our agonist+PAM bound structure is consistent with the recently reported active conformation of the Ca2+/L-Trp-bound structure of CaSR (CaSRAcc) (Ling et al., 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the structure reported by Ling et al., 2021, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D.

claim: In the inactive structure, there is only one interface at the apex of the receptor and the VFT module adopts an open conformation with the nanobody binding at the left lateral side of each LB2 domain.
source: In the inactive structure, there is only one interface at the apex of the receptor and the VFT module adopts an open conformation with the nanobody binding at the left lateral side of each LB2 domain (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: The active state has the overall buried surface area of 3378 Å2, whereas it substantially decreases to 1346 Å2 in the inactive state.
source: The active state has the overall buried surface area of 3378 Å2, whereas it substantially decreases to 1346 Å2 in the inactive state (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Comparing the inactive open–open conformation (CaSRfully inactive) with CaSRIcc revealed similar 7TM domains, but two totally different VFT module conformations.
source: Comparing our inactive open–open conformation (CaSRfully inactive) with their CaSRIcc revealed similar 7TM domains, but two totally different VFT module conformations, with their closed–closed conformation presenting similar characteristics to the active state (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The CaSRIcc closed–closed conformation presents similar characteristics to the active state.
source: Comparing our inactive open–open conformation (CaSRfully inactive) with their CaSRIcc revealed similar 7TM domains, but two totally different VFT module conformations, with their closed–closed conformation presenting similar characteristics to the active state (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: In addition to the full inactive state and the active state, there are multiple intermediate states in the process of activation of CaSR.
source: This indicates that the CaSR in the inactive state has conformational heterogeneity. In other words, this suggests that in addition to the full inactive state and the active state, there are multiple intermediate states in the process of activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of conformational heterogeneity in the structures.

claim: Three distinct Ca2+-binding sites were identified within ECD of each protomer in the active state.
source: The high-resolution density of active state map enabled us to identify three distinct Ca2+-binding sites within ECD of each protomer (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two Ca2+-binding sites were previously reported.
source: Two sites were previously reported (Geng et al., 2016; Ling et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A new Ca2+-binding site was found at the interdomain cleft of the VFT module that is close to the hinge loop and abuts the TNCA binding site.
source: while a new Ca2+-binding site was found at the interdomain cleft of the VFT module that is close to the hinge loop and abuts the TNCA binding site, and interacts with both LB1 and LB2 domains to facilitate ECD closure (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: The new Ca2+-binding site interacts with both LB1 and LB2 domains to facilitate ECD closure.
source: while a new Ca2+-binding site was found at the interdomain cleft of the VFT module that is close to the hinge loop and abuts the TNCA binding site, and interacts with both LB1 and LB2 domains to facilitate ECD closure (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: The bound Ca2+ ion is primarily coordinated with side chains of D190 and E297, carbonyl oxygen atoms of P188 backbone, and hydroxyl groups of S170 and Y489.
source: The bound Ca2+ ion is primarily coordinated with side chains of D190 and E297, carbonyl oxygen atoms of P188 backbone, and hydroxyl groups of S170 and Y489.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Residues P188, D190, and S170 are located in LB1 domain, while E297 and Y489 are in LB2.
source: Residues P188, D190, and S170 are located in LB1 domain, while E297 and Y489 are in LB2 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The main coordination residues (S170, D190, and E297) of the Ca2+ ion are consistent with those previously reported.
source: The main coordination residues (S170, D190, and E297) of the Ca2+ ion are consistent with those previously reported (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study cited.

claim: Single mutation of residues D190K, S170K, E297K, and Y489F significantly reduced the effect of Ca2+-stimulated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells.
source: Third, the main binding residues (S170, D190, and E297) of Ca2+ ion were previously reported (Liu et al., 2020), and that single mutation of these residues (D190K, S170K and E297K, and Y489F) significantly reduced the effect of Ca2+-stimulated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The cell surface expression levels of mutants D190K, S170K, E297K, and Y489F are all above 80% compared to the wild-type level.
source: The cell surface expression levels of these mutants are all above 80% compared to the wild-type level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutant of residue S147A largely impaired the Ca2+ effect.
source: Finally, mutant of a residue that bind L-amino acid (S147A) also largely impaired the Ca2+ effect (Geng et al., 2016), indicating the presence of L-amino acid near Ca2+ ion and that Ca2+ activates CaSR through the L-amino acid.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2016.

claim: The binding details of TNCA were the same as previously reported data.
source: The binding details of TNCA were the same as previously reported data (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study.

claim: The interactions between TNCA and VFT are primarily mediated by hydrogen bonds.
source: The interactions between TNCA and VFT are primarily mediated by hydrogen bonds (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The bound Ca2+ and TNCA share three common binding residues S170, D190, and E297.
source: It is interesting that our structure shows that the bound Ca2+ and TNCA share three common binding residues S170, D190, and E297 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Each of single mutations S170A, D190K, and E297K abolishes Ca2+-dependent receptor response.
source: Our experiment has shown that each of single mutations S170A, D190K, and E297K abolishes Ca2+-dependent receptor response (Figure 3E), consistent with Liu et al., 2020.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ increases L-Trp binding.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the extracellular Ca2+ increases L-Trp binding (Geng et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: L-Trp directly stimulates intracellular Ca2+ mobilization through CaSR.
source: and L-Trp also directly stimulates intracellular Ca2+ mobilization through CaSR (Conigrave et al., 2004; Rey et al., 2005; Young and Rozengurt, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The efficacy and potency of L-Trp increase with increase in Ca2+ concentration.
source: and the efficacy and potency of L-Trp increase with increase in Ca2+ concentration (Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: L-amino acids increase the effect of Ca2+ ions on the CaSR.
source: As mentioned above, L-amino acids increase the effect of Ca2+ ions on the CaSR (Jensen and Brauner-Osborne, 2007; Liu et al., 2020; Quinn et al., 2004; Saidak et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: TNCA potentiate the Ca2+ activity.
source: and TNCA potentiate the Ca2+ activity (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CaSR is synergistically activated by the composite agonist composed of TNCA and Ca2+ ions.
source: Altogether, we show that CaSR is synergistically activated by the composite agonist composed of TNCA and Ca2+ ions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data presented in the study.

claim: TNCA directly activated CaSR in the presence of 0.5 mM of Ca2+ ions with EC50 of 2.839 mM.
source: Using intracellular Ca2+ flux assays, we found that TNCA directly activated CaSR in the presence of 0.5 mM of Ca2+ ions and that the effect on CaSR was concentration-dependent with EC50 of 2.839 mM (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: L-Trp directly stimulated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells stably expressing CaSR using single-cell intracellular Ca2+ microfluorimetry.
source: in agreement with previous reports that L-Trp directly stimulated intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells stably expressing CaSR using single-cell intracellular Ca2+ microfluorimetry (Geng et al., 2016; Rey et al., 2005; Young and Rozengurt, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interface of LB1–LB1 dimer is predominantly a hydrophobic core formed by residues on two central helices (B and C) of each protomer.
source: Both inactive and active structures reveal that the interface of LB1–LB1 dimer is predominantly a hydrophobic core, which is formed by the residues on two central helices (B and C) of each protomer, including V115, V149, as well as L156 for inactive structure and L112, L156, L159, and F160 for active crystal structure (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the structures shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The B–C helix angle has rotated approximately 28° from inactive state (117°) to active state (89°).
source: On the dimer interfaces, The B–C helix angle has rotated approximately 28° from inactive state (117°) to active state (89°) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Liu et al. detected reorientation of LB1–LB1 dimer during activation using a FRET-based conformation CaSR sensor.
source: Our result is in line with earlier reports of CaSR and other class C GPCRs activation. Liu et al. detected reorientation of LB1–LB1 dimer during activation using a FRET-based conformation CaSR sensor (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: mGluR5 receptor changes from active to apo state with an approximately 59° rotation of the B–C helix angle.
source: mGluR5 receptor changes from active to apo state with an approximately 59° rotation of the B–C helix angle (Koehl et al., 2019; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koehl et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: No rotation of B–C helix was observed between inactive CaSR-ECDIoo and active CaSR-ECDactive crystal structures.
source: We then compared the B-C helix angles of previously reported CaSR structures, including CaSR-ECDIoo, CaSR-ECDactive, CaSRIcc, and CaSRAcc. No rotation of B–C helix was observed between inactive CaSR-ECDIoo and active CaSR-ECDactive crystal structures (Figure 4B; Geng et al., 2016)
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was only a small rotation of 1° between CaSRIcc and CaSRAcc.
source: Similarly, there was only a small rotation of 1° between CaSRIcc and CaSRAcc (Figure 4C; Ling et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structures shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The B–C Helix angle of all four reported structures (CaSR-ECDIoo, CaSR-ECDactive, CaSRIcc, CaSRAcc) resemble that of the active CaSRagonist+PAM structure.
source: The B–C Helix angle of all four reported structures (CaSR-ECDIoo, CaSR-ECDactive, CaSRIcc, CaSRAcc) resemble that of our active CaSRagonist+PAM structure (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structures shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The reported conformations (CaSR-ECDIoo, CaSRIcc) should be considered intermediate states in the activation process of CaSR because they exhibit some characteristics of the active state.
source: In summary, we propose that these reported conformations should be considered intermediate states in the activation process of CaSR because they exhibit some characteristics of the active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural comparisons.

claim: The inactive cryo-EM structure represents the full inactive state of CaSR.
source: Therefore, our inactive cryo-EM structure represents the full inactive state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data.

claim: The conformational transition of the LB1 domain from inactive to intermediate state provides the structural basis for ligand binding.
source: Thus, the conformational transition of the LB1 domain from inactive to intermediate state provides the structural basis for ligand binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons.

claim: No significant difference of the overall LB2 conformations is observed among the superposition of inactive, intermediate (CaSR-ECDIoo), and agonist+PAM bound structures.
source: No significant difference of the overall LB2 conformations is observed among the superposition of inactive, intermediate (CaSR-ECDIoo), and agonist+PAM bound structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of CaSR in inactive state displays a relatively large backbone separation distance of 56.26 Å between the C-terminal ends of N541 of each LB2 domain.
source: The cryo-EM structure of CaSR in inactive state displays a relatively large backbone separation distance of 56.26 Å between the C-terminal ends of N541 of each LB2 domain, while it reduces to 45.8 Å in the CaSRIoo state and 41.8 Å in the CaSRIcc state. A further reduction to 29 Å is observed upon activation in the active model (Figure 5).
evidence: This is measured from the structures shown in Figure 5.

claim: The two LB2 domains gradually approach each other until they interact, a process that is not induced by the agonists.
source: Thus, the two LB2 domains gradually approach each other until they interact, a process that is not induced by the agonists (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: NB-2D11 binds the left lateral of each LB2 domain from orthogonal view.
source: The inactive structure reveals that NB-2D11 binds the left lateral of each LB2 domain from orthogonal view (Figure 6)
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: The hydrophilic interaction interface between NB-2D11 and CaSR involves amino acids D53, D99, W102, R101, and E110 from CDR1 and CDR3 of the nanobody and residues R220, S240, S244, Y246, S247, and E251 from Helix F and Strand I of CaSR.
source: with the hydrophilic interaction interface between the amino acids D53, D99, W102, R101, and E110 from CDR1 and CDR3 of the nanobody and the residues R220, S240, S244, Y246, S247, and E251 from Helix F and Strand I (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NB-D211 occupies the spatial position of the LB2 domain of the other protomer, which blocks the approach of another corresponding subunit LB2.
source: Superposition of the inactive and agonist+PAM bound LB2 domains shows that NB-D211 occupies the spatial position of the LB2 domain of the other protomer, which blocks the approach of another corresponding subunit LB2 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is observed from the structural superposition shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The interactions of both LB2 domains are required to activate CaSR.
source: Our results indicate that the interactions of both LB2 domains are required to activate CaSR, which is the explanation of the inhibitory function of NB-2D11.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The closure of VFT displays an inward rotation of each LB2 followed by moving upward individually.
source: The closure of VFT displays an inward rotation of each LB2 followed by moving upward individually (Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed in the structural transition shown in Figure 5.

claim: Two intersubunit interfaces are formed at the downstream of subunits during activation, including the interaction between the LB2 linked CRDs and the intersubunit interaction between TMDs.
source: Afterwards, two intersubunit interfaces are formed at the downstream of subunits, including the interaction between the LB2 linked CRDs, which is consistent with the reported crystal structure of CaSR ECD (Geng et al., 2016; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and the intersubunit interaction between TMDs (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is observed in the structures shown in Figure 7A–F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inactive structure reveals that TM5 and TM6 constitute a 7TMD plane–plane interface.
source: The inactive structure reveals that TM5 and TM6 constitute a 7TMD plane–plane interface (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There are pairwise symmetrical undefined maps that link the extracellular and intracellular part of TM5 and TM6 in the 7TMD interface.
source: There are pairwise symmetrical undefined maps that link the extracellular and intracellular part of TM5 and TM6 in the 7TMD interface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Each of the single mutations F789A or F792A attenuates Ca2+-induced receptor activity.
source: Our experiments show that each of the single mutations F789A or F792A attenuates Ca2+-induced receptor activity, indicating that this contact plays a role in the activation of CaSR (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: The agonist+PAM bound structure shows a TM6–TM6 interface, contacting at the apex of TM6 helices, which is a hallmark of GPCR activation.
source: The agonist+PAM bound structure shows a TM6–TM6 interface, contacting at the apex of TM6 helices, which is a hallmark of GPCR activation (Koehl et al., 2019; Figure 7B,F).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 7B,F and supported by citation to Koehl et al., 2019.

claim: Mutation to P823 in TM6 markedly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity.
source: To further validate the role of this interface, mutation to P823 in TM6 markedly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity (Figure 7J), indicating that the TM6–TM6 interface is crucial to CaSR activation, consistent with previous studies.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Liu et al. reported an interface mediated by TM6 in their active CaSR structure and showed that a cysteine cross-linking at residue A8246.56 in TM6 led to a constitutively active receptor.
source: Liu et al. reported an interface mediated by TM6 in their active CaSR structure and showed that a cysteine cross-linking at residue A8246.56 in TM6 led to a constitutively active receptor (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Active mGluR5 and GABAB receptors have the same TM6–TM6 interface.
source: Similarly, active mGluR5 (Koehl et al., 2019) and GABAB receptors (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020) have the same TM6–TM6 interface (Figure 7F; Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: TM6 cross-linked mGluR5 and TM6-locked mGluR2 were activated continuously.
source: TM6 cross-linked mGluR5 and TM6-locked mGluR2 were activated continuously (Koehl et al., 2019; Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A small rotation of LB2 domains could propagate to large-scale transitions of the TMDs through the CRDs, thereby reorientating the 7TMDs from the inactive plane–plane interface mediated by TM5 and TM6 to the active interface driven by TM6.
source: Therefore, a small rotation of LB2 domains could propagate to large-scale transitions of the TMDs through the CRDs, thereby reorientating the 7TMDs from the inactive plane–plane interface mediated by TM5 and TM6 to the active interface driven by TM6 (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data shown in Figure 7E–G.

claim: The proximity of 7TMDs is observed during the activation, from a plane–plane distance of 24 Å in inactive state to 5.7 Å at P8236.55 in the active state.
source: The proximity of 7TMDs is observed during the activation, from a plane–plane distance of 24 Å in inactive state to 5.7 Å at P8236.55 in the active state (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).

claim: There is a bundle of structure in the junction region between extracellular and transmembrane domain, which is composed of C-terminal elongated peptide of CRD and the twisted hairpin loop of ECL2.
source: Models of both inactive and active structures reveal that there is a bundle of structure in the junction region between extracellular and transmembrane domain, which is composed of C-terminal elongated peptide of CRD and the twisted hairpin loop of ECL2 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the structures shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: The residues 759–763 fragment of ECL2 and the C-terminal residues of the CRD (601–604) form a new interface in the agonist+PAM bound state.
source: The structure of the agonist+PAM bound state shows that the residues 759–763 fragment of ECL2 and the C-terminal residues of the CRD (601–604) form a new interface (Figure 8A)
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the agonist+PAM bound state, the loop of ECL2 is pulled up by the interaction among E759, W590, and K601, leading to the movement of ECL2.
source: In the agonist+PAM bound state, the loop of ECL2 is pulled up by the interaction among E759, W590, and K601, leading to the movement of ECL2 (Figure 8)
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 8.

claim: Deletion of residues D758 and E759 at the apex of ECL2 led to a significantly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity.
source: To confirm the importance of this interaction, deletion of residues D758 and E759 at the apex of ECL2 (Figure 8D), as well as single mutations of K601E and W590E (Figure 8E,F), disrupted these contacts and led to a significantly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Single mutations of K601E and W590E disrupted the contacts between CRD and ECL2 and led to a significantly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity.
source: To confirm the importance of this interaction, deletion of residues D758 and E759 at the apex of ECL2 (Figure 8D), as well as single mutations of K601E and W590E (Figure 8E,F), disrupted these contacts and led to a significantly reduced Ca2+-induced receptor activity
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: ECL2 plays a key role in relaying the conformational changes of VFT to the intrasubunit TM domain to rearrange the structure to adapt to downstream transducers, such as G proteins.
source: Therefore, ECL2 plays a key role in relaying the conformational changes of VFT to the intrasubunit TM domain to rearrange the structure to adapt to downstream transducers, such as G proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The B–C helix angle at the interfaces of LB1–LB1 dimer sharply rotated from inactive to active state during receptor activation.
source: Multiple structural and functional studies of class C GPCR have demonstrated that there are two typical conformational changes in the VFT domains during receptor activation. One is that the B–C helix angle at the interfaces of LB1–LB1 dimer sharply rotated from inactive to active state.
evidence: This is based on multiple structural and functional studies of class C GPCRs.

claim: The conformational transition of the LB1 domain is conducive to ligand binding, which is a prerequisite for receptor activation.
source: This conformational transition of the LB1 domain is conducive to ligand binding, which is a prerequisite for receptor activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Increased glutamate affinity and occupancy in mGluR2 active conformation were observed by the mutations in B-Helix.
source: For example, increased glutamate affinity and occupancy in mGluR2 active conformation were observed by the mutations in B-Helix (Levitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levitz et al., 2016.

claim: The conformation of VFT domain is converted from open to closed for the change of interdomain in one protomer, which is a landmark event during receptor activation.
source: Another is that the conformation of VFT domain is converted from open to closed for the change of interdomain in one protomer, which is a landmark event during receptor activation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of class C GPCR activation.

claim: The VFT domain rearranged from open–open configuration to closed–closed configuration during CaSR activation.
source: The B–C helix angle has rotated approximately 28° from inactive to agonist+PAM bound state and the VFT domain rearranged from open–open configuration to closed–closed configuration during CaSR activation (Figures 4A and 5)
evidence: This is observed in the structures shown in Figures 4A and 5.

claim: The CaSR dimer underwent a large conformational change of LB1–LB1 dimer during activation, in which the B–C helix angle rotated from inactive to active state.
source: In addition, Liu et al. developed a FRET-based conformation sensor for CaSR through fusion of SNAP-tag at its N-terminus of CaSR subunit to label with fluorophores. Their data showed that the CaSR dimer underwent a large conformational change of LB1–LB1 dimer during activation, in which the B–C helix angle rotated from inactive to active state as the fluorophores labeled the N-terminus of LB1 domain (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: The rotation of LB1–LB1 domains is a watershed between inactive and intermediate states.
source: The rotation of LB1–LB1 domains is a watershed between inactive and intermediate states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: Both CaSR-ECDIoo and CaSRIcc are different intermediate states during the activation of CaSR.
source: It is likely that both CaSR-ECDIoo and CaSRIcc are different intermediate states during the activation of CaSR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: The prevailing view is that the principal agonist of CaSR is extracellular Ca2+.
source: At present, the prevailing view is that the principal agonist of CaSR is extracellular Ca2+ (Hofer and Brown, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hofer and Brown, 2003.

claim: L-amino acids, such as L-Trp, can enhance the sensitivity of CaSR toward Ca2+ ions and are considered as PAMs of the receptor.
source: L-amino acids, such as L-Trp, can enhance the sensitivity of CaSR toward Ca2+ ions (Conigrave et al., 2000), and are considered as PAMs of the receptor (Saidak et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A FRET study showed that Ca2+ ions are sufficient to activate CaSR in the absence of L-amino acids.
source: In line with this view, a recently reported FRET study showed that Ca2+ ions are sufficient to activate CaSR in the absence of L-amino acids, such that Ca2+ could be considered as an agonist of CaSR, whereas L-amino acids are pure PAMs of CaSR (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: If Ca2+ concentration is higher than the threshold of 0.5 mM, L-amino acid can activate the receptor.
source: In contrast, some studies have also shown that if Ca2+ concentration is higher than the threshold of 0.5 mM, L-amino acid can activate the receptor (Conigrave et al., 2004; Conigrave et al., 2000; Rey et al., 2005; Young and Rozengurt, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ca2+ and L-amino acid can act as co-agonists of the receptor.
source: indicating that Ca2+ and L-amino acid can act as co-agonists of the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the studies showing that L-amino acids can activate the receptor in the presence of Ca2+.

claim: L-Trp has been shown to directly stimulate intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells stably expressing CaSR, with its efficacy and potency increase with increases in concentration of Ca2+ ions.
source: Using single-cell intracellular Ca2+ microfluorimetry, L-Trp has been shown to directly stimulate intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in cells stably expressing CaSR, with its efficacy and potency increase with increases in concentration of Ca2+ ions, hence providing direct evidence that L-amino acids are agonists of CaSR (Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2016.

claim: TNCA binds at the cleft between LB1 and LB2 domains, which is the binding site for all class C GPCR agonists.
source: The structure of CaSR shows that TNCA binds at the cleft between LB1 and LB2 domains, which is the binding site for all class C GPCR agonists (Geng et al., 2013; Geng et al., 2016; Kunishima et al., 2000; Muto et al., 2007; Tsuchiya et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TNCA has a binding pattern similar to that of the endogenous agonists of mGluR and GABAB receptors.
source: and TNCA has a binding pattern similar to that of the endogenous agonists of mGluR and GABAB receptors (Figure 3D; Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation to Geng et al., 2016.

claim: The key coordination residues for TNCA binding are very conserved, such as S147 and S170.
source: The key coordination residues are very conserved, such as S147 and S170 (Geng et al., 2013; Geng et al., 2016; Kunishima et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TNCA (or L-Trp) interact with residues from LB1 and LB2 to stabilize the closure of VFT.
source: Moreover, TNCA (or L-Trp) interact with residues from LB1 and LB2 to stabilize the closure of VFT
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The signal mutation of the contacting residues (T145I, S147A, S170A, Y218S, E297K) substantially reduce the function of the receptor.
source: and the signal mutation of the contacting residues (T145I, S147A, S170A, Y218S, E297K) substantially reduce the function of the receptor, even if some of these residues (S147A, T145I, and Y218S) are not related to the coordinating residues of Ca2+, hence indicating that TNCA or L-Trp plays a key role in the activation of CaSR (Geng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2016.

claim: Ling et al. did not obtain the closed conformation of VFT containing only Ca2+ ion between the cleft.
source: However, they did not obtain the closed conformation of VFT containing only Ca2+ ion between the cleft (Ling et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the results reported by Ling et al., 2021.

claim: Ca2+ ion alone is not enough to induce the closure of the VFT module even in the presence of a high concentration of Ca2+ ion.
source: The results indicate that Ca2+ ion alone is not enough to induce the closure of the VFT module even in the presence of a high concentration of Ca2+ ion, and L-amino acid or its derivate is required to stabilize the closed conformation of VFT module.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of Ling et al., 2021.

claim: L-amino acid or its derivate is required to stabilize the closed conformation of VFT module.
source: The results indicate that Ca2+ ion alone is not enough to induce the closure of the VFT module even in the presence of a high concentration of Ca2+ ion, and L-amino acid or its derivate is required to stabilize the closed conformation of VFT module.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of Ling et al., 2021.

claim: L-amino acids are the endogenous agonists of CaSR, in agreement with that of other class C GPCRs.
source: Altogether, L-amino acids are the endogenous agonists of CaSR, in agreement with that of other class C GPCRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data.

claim: Three different groups prepared CaSR samples without L-amino acids or derivatives for crystal or cryo-EM structural studies, but they all unexpectedly obtained the active structure of CaSR or CaSR ECD with closed–closed VFT conformation containing undefined ligands.
source: Three different groups prepared CaSR samples without L-amino acids or derivatives for crystal or cryo-EM structural studies, but they all unexpectedly obtained the active structure of CaSR or CaSR ECD with closed–closed VFT conformation containing undefined ligands (Geng et al., 2016; Ling et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TNCA had a high affinity for CaSR, and potentiated Ca2+ activity.
source: This ligand was subsequently identified as TNCA, which had a high affinity for CaSR, and potentiated Ca2+ activity (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: TNCA tightly binds to CaSR or is buried in closed VFT module such that it is difficult to be washed off.
source: This indicates that TNCA tightly binds to CaSR or that it is buried in closed VFT module such that it is difficult to be washed off.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TNCA is found in structures prepared without added L-amino acids.

claim: Ca2+ ion is coordinated by D234, E231, and G557, and bridges the LB2 domain of one subunit and the CR domain of the second subunit.
source: In addition to the role of Ca2+ ion binding at the cleft of VFT module to stabilize the closed conformation of VFT, another role of the Ca2+ ions should be considered, in which Ca2+ ion is coordinated by D234, E231, and G557, and bridges the LB2 domain of one subunit and the CR domain of the second subunit.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Ca2+ ion facilitates the formation of the active conformation of CaSR.
source: Ca2+ ion facilitates the formation of the active conformation of CaSR, which explain why L-amino acids (or TNCA) can activate CaSR in the presence of Ca2+ ion above the threshold concentration of 0.5 mM.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The proximity of both LB2 domains is an automatic process rather than an agonist-driven one.
source: Although we do not have a fully active conformation of the CaSR without agonist binding as evidence, crystal structures of a fully closed VFT modules of mGluR1 with or without agonist binding were previously reported (Kunishima et al., 2000) and have demonstrated that the proximity of both LB2 domains is an automatic process rather than an agonist-driven one.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kunishima et al., 2000.

claim: NB-2D11 inhibited CaSR activation by blocking the proximity of both LB2 domains.
source: Here, we showed that NB-2D11 inhibited CaSR activation by blocking the proximity of both LB2 domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data.

claim: Liu et al. observed a TM4–TM5-plane/TM4–TM5-plane interface in the inactive state, but a TM6–TM6 contact in the active state of the CaSR dimer.
source: Liu et al. used FRET sensor to investigate the 7TM interface rearrangement during the activation of the CaSR through a disulfide cross-linking approach. They observed a TM4–TM5-plane/TM4–TM5-plane interface in the inactive state, but a TM6–TM6 contact in the active state of the CaSR dimer (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: The conformational heterogeneity of the interface of 7TMDs in the inactive state indicates that there is a possible dynamic equilibrium between the TM4–TM5 and TM5–TM6 interfaces.
source: The conformational heterogeneity of the interface of 7TMDs in the inactive state indicates that there is a possible dynamic equilibrium between the TM4–TM5 and TM5–TM6 interfaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different interfaces in different studies.

claim: TM6–TM6 contact in the active state is considered to be a hallmark of class C GPCR activation.
source: TM6–TM6 contact in the active state is considered to be a hallmark of class C GPCR activation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of class C GPCR activation.

source: For mGluR5 and GABAB receptors, the 7TMDs rearrange from TM5–TM5 interface in the inactive state to TM6–TM6 interface in the active state (Kim et al., 2020; Koehl et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2020; Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It is possible that the undefined maps between the 7TMD in the full inactive structure could be sterols that separate the dimer plane–plane interface and stabilize the inactive state.
source: It is possible that the undefined maps between the 7TMD in our full inactive structure could be sterols that separate the dimer plane–plane interface and stabilize the inactive state (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of undefined density and comparison with GABAB receptor structures.

claim: The alignment of individual 7TM of both inactive and agonist+PAM states shows that the helices are well superposed, indicating that the change of ECL2 conformation is unable to drive the rearrangements of TM4 and TM5 helices and stabilize the active conformation in the TMDs.
source: However, the alignment of individual 7TM of both inactive and agonist+PAM states shows that the helices are well superposed, indicating that the change of ECL2 conformation is unable to drive the rearrangements of TM4 and TM5 helices and stabilize the active conformation in the TMDs (Koehl et al., 2019)
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison and supported by citation to Koehl et al., 2019.

claim: The active state of mGluR5 is stabilized by G proteins.
source: This observation is consistent with findings that the active state of mGluR5 is stabilized by G proteins (Koehl et al., 2019; Manglik et al., 2015; Rosenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.
